Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 67
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Military Medic
  trauma_type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
  pcl5: 64

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident, Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Thought Monitoring: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy, Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
  Memory: Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted, Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person

Vignette:
Frank, at sixty-seven, found that his world had shrunk to the four walls of his small suburban home. A widower for five years and a retired Army medic, he had always defined himself by his competence and steady hand. That definition shattered six months ago on a rain-slicked road. He had been driving home from a weekly poker game when headlights swerved into his lane. The memory of the event rarely came to him as a coherent story. When he tried to explain it to his son, the words would falter and the thread would vanish, leaving him staring at the wall, unable to articulate the sequence of the crash. The images that did come felt distant, as if he were watching a film about a stranger. In these flashes, he wasn't an active participant but a helpless observer of another man’s tragedy. The only parts that felt truly his were the sounds that ambushed him in the quiet of the night: the sickening crunch of metal and the final, sharp pop of the other car’s tire, replaying with startling clarity in his mind.

He was certain the collision was his fault. He’d spent a career making split-second, life-or-death decisions, and in that critical moment, he had failed. He replayed it constantly, convinced that a different turn of the wheel, a half-second sooner on the brake, would have changed the outcome. This deep-seated conviction that he had acted wrongly had poisoned his trust in himself. He now questioned every minor decision, from what to buy at the grocery store to whether he’d locked the front door, certain he could no longer rely on his own judgment to do the right thing. This constant self-doubt felt like a profound personal failing, a confirmation of a weakness he never knew he possessed.

His days became a series of careful navigations around potential reminders. The smell of something burning, even just a piece of toast in his own kitchen, would send a jolt of panic through him, his heart pounding in his chest as he was mentally thrown back to the sight of smoke billowing from the other car’s engine. He stopped watching the local news after a report on a highway pile-up left him breathless and shaking. The most potent trigger, however, was the smell of alcohol. When he had stumbled from his own wrecked vehicle that night, his training taking over, he had been met with the overwhelming stench of whiskey from the other driver. Now, if a neighbor was having a barbecue and the scent of beer drifted over the fence, his body would tense as if for impact.

To manage this constant threat, Frank had systematically dismantled his old life. He sold his car three months ago, telling his son it was just too expensive to maintain. The truth was that the thought of getting behind the wheel, or even sitting in the passenger seat, was unbearable. This decision had consequences. He could no longer make his volunteer shifts at the VA hospital, a loss that deepened his sense of uselessness. He tried to force the intrusive thoughts and sounds from his mind, but the effort was exhausting, a constant battle he always seemed to lose. He lived in a state of hypervigilance, and the slightest unexpected noise—a door slamming down the street, a dish dropped in the kitchen—would cause him to jump so violently he’d feel his muscles ache afterward. He began to monitor his own mind with a grim intensity, listening to the fragmented memories and the internal chaos, terrified it was all a sign that he was losing his grip on reality.

It was after he missed his grandson’s school play because he couldn’t bring himself to get a ride that he finally made a call for an appointment. He came to therapy not with a clear path forward, but with a quiet, desperate fear. He felt broken, a weak and unreliable version of the man he once was. What he hoped for, more than anything, was to silence the sounds in his head and to once again feel like he could trust himself to navigate the world.
